articles.title: Charting the evolution of human–machine communication: a systematic review of 25 years of empirical research
articles.authors: Fanjue Liu, Xiaobei Chen, Kun Xu
articles.abstract: This study systematically examines trends and patterns in human–machine communication (HMC) research from 2000 to 2024. Based on a comprehensive screening of studies published in 28 communication and interdisciplinary journals and 2 foundational books, we analyzed 209 peer-reviewed articles based on their metadata, theoretical frameworks, research methods, technologies of interest, and research themes. The findings show steady growth in HMC scholarship following its formal recognition as a subfield with the establishment of the ICA Interest Group in 2019, continued reliance on social scientific research designs, and increasing interdisciplinary contributions. A BERTopic analysis identified 9 coherent research clusters, reflecting a gradual shift from robot-focused investigations toward a broader range of studies on virtual agents, chatbots, and generative AI. Overall, this review maps HMC’s intellectual trajectory and highlights key directions for future theoretical, methodological, and interdisciplinary development. It also discusses the increasingly ambiguous boundaries of HMC given the growing use of large language models and the convergent spaces between HMC and AI-mediated communication.

articles.title: Utopian media studies: Introduction
articles.authors: Steve Jankowski, Jakko Kemper
articles.abstract: This introduction to the special issue ‘Utopian Media Studies’ sketches a framework for how media studies can become a site of utopian praxis, research and experimentation. It first addresses three apprehensions media scholars might have about the notion of utopian media studies and its appeal to a loaded concept like ‘utopia’. The introduction then outlines five sensibilities to explicate the nature and significance of this special issue’s contribution to the field: a utopian media studies must adopt an ecological approach to media; recognize and be invigorated by limits; work toward the technological liberation of time; connect imagination with practice; and emphasize and enable conditions for transmitting hope. Lastly, the introduction considers Ruth Levitas’s distinction between utopia’s archaeological, ontological, and architectural mode to map some of the concrete ways in which existing media studies research is doing utopian work that aligns with these sensibilities. In connecting work that operates in these modes with the various contributions to this special issue, the introduction reveals the utopian currents that already run through media studies as a discipline and opens up new conceptual and methodological approaches to studying and modeling digital utopias.

articles.title: Negotiating the platform turn: Genre, format, and co-production in RTP’s fiction strategy
articles.authors: Gabriela Orestes
articles.abstract: This article investigates how Portugal’s public service broadcaster, Rádio e Televisão de Portugal (RTP), has adapted its fiction strategies over the past two decades, contrasting the pre-platform period (2005–2014) with the platform era following the entry of global streaming services into the Portuguese market (2015–2024). Drawing on platformisation theory and scholarship on small-market public service media (PSM), the study employs a mixed-methods, longitudinal approach, combining quantitative analysis of RTP1’s fiction output, qualitative content analysis of two series, and a semi-structured, exploratory interview with the programming director. Findings show that traditional pressures – such as limited budgets, small audience scale, and market constraints – were reconfigured in the platform era, generating both challenges and opportunities for innovation. Key strategies included a shift from horizontal to vertical scheduling, the increased production of medium-form series, an expansion of drama and crime genres, and selective transnational co-productions with global platforms. The study highlights how platformisation transforms content strategies in peripheral media systems, producing context-specific forms of constraint and creativity, and offers new insights into the adaptive capacities of small-market PSM in the digital streaming era.

articles.title: Layered Censorship: Platform logics and the governance of taboo in religious Media
articles.authors: Efrat Refaeli, Motti Neiger
articles.abstract: This article examines how the governance of taboo issues is reconfigured across platformized communication environments. Drawing on a qualitative comparative analysis of the Walder affair—a moral crisis in Israeli Ultra-Orthodox society that erupted in November 2021 and culminated in the subject's suicide in December of that year—it analyzes how five distinct communication arenas managed allegations of sexual abuse against a prominent religious figure. The findings demonstrate that censorship does not operate as a unified institutional mechanism but as a distributed configuration of communicative practices. Different arenas adopted distinct modes of managing taboo information: institutional silence, normative enforcement, discursive displacement, selective disclosure, and contested openness. These variations reflect the communicative logics, institutional arrangements, and participation structures associated with different communication arenas. To account for these dynamics, the article introduces the concept of Layered Censorship: a platform-differentiated configuration of communicative practices through which taboo information is suppressed, displaced, selectively disclosed, morally regulated, and publicly contested across a shared media ecology. The concept highlights how different communication arenas perform distinct regulatory functions while occupying different positions along a continuum of discursive openness. By conceptualizing censorship as a distributed and differentiated form of communicative governance, the article offers a framework applicable beyond religious contexts to other highly regulated communication environments.

articles.title: Extremists Play Games Too: Gaming References in Extremist Discourse
articles.authors: Neven Vukic
articles.abstract: The “gamification of terror” has become a dominant lens for interpreting links between video games and extremism. This article challenges that consensus through a Critical Discourse Analysis of the manifestos of Anders Breivik, Brenton Tarrant, and Elliot Rodger, triangulated with official investigations including the Gjørv Report, the Royal Commission of Inquiry, and law-enforcement case files. The analysis finds no uniform pathway between gaming and radicalization. Instead, gaming assumes three context-specific roles: Sanctuary (an emotional refuge from social failure), Vernacular (a stylistic register rather than an ideological source), or Alibi (a strategic cover for operational preparation). In Rodger's case, an inverse pattern emerges: his radicalization escalated only after he abandoned gaming as sanctuary. These findings indicate that current P/CVE frameworks may misidentify gameplay as a risk factor, while more meaningful indicators lie in abrupt withdrawals from gaming or conflicts such as griefing that destabilize existing online routines.

articles.title: Playing the Museum: Videogame Heritage, Interactivity, and Cultural Legitimacy
articles.authors: Jorge Pérez, Yoel Villahermosa Serrano
articles.abstract: This article examines the emergence of videogame museums in Spain through a comparative analysis of MUVI Museo do Videoxogo Galego in Cangas, the Museo del Videojuego Arcade Vintage in Ibi, and the OXO Videogame Museums in Málaga and Madrid. It argues that these institutions are shaped by an informational-interactive dilemma: they must preserve, explain, and legitimize videogames as cultural heritage while also allowing visitors to play, touch, and experience them as interactive media. Rather than treating this tension as a problem to be solved, the article shows how different curatorial models translate the complex nature of games into spatial, educational, commercial, and participatory practices. Videogame museums do not simply exhibit objects; they negotiate among software, hardware, play, memory, authorship, community, and cultural value. In doing so, they actively define what videogames are, what counts as videogame heritage, and how games enter the museum.

articles.title: Creating mental imagery of cultural creative product with AR: a mixed-methods study of the affordances and consumer responses
articles.authors: Bin Li, Zhou Qi
articles.abstract: Purpose Cultural and creative products is embracing augmented reality (AR) as a new opportunity to explain traditional culture and revitalize heritage marketing. However, effects and psychological mechanisms of this intersection remain underexplored. This study draws upon affordance perspective and develops a conceptual framework based on mental imagery theory, aiming to elucidate affordances and consumer responses of AR cultural creative products through a mixed-methods design. Design/methodology/approach Firstly, this study investigates affordances of AR (i.e. aesthetics, functionality, symbolism, interactivity and symbiosis) that enables cultural representation through interviews. Subsequently, a cross-sectional survey demonstrates the performance of AR. Findings The affordances of AR (i.e. aesthetics, functionality, symbolism, interactivity and symbiosis) help consumers to build mental imagery (i.e. elaboration and quality) of the culture and psychological proximity, contributing to positive outcome (i.e. consumer satisfaction, purchase intention and cultural identification). Originality/value These findings offer insights into AR research and provide practical guidance on how to deploy AR for cultural and creative products.

articles.title: Technoshame: emotional challenges related to technology-mediated feedback in online work
articles.authors: Pernille Steen Pedersen, Sine Zambach, Ad de Jong
articles.abstract: Purpose This article explores emotional challenges experienced by university educators when teaching fully online. Drawing on the theoretical framework of organizational shame, we introduce technoshame to capture how technology-mediated feedback in online settings may trigger perceived inadequacy and pose a threat to one's professional identity in online work settings. Design/methodology/approach The study is based on an exploratory design combining qualitative interviews with university faculty with quantitative survey data. Data collection was conducted during two COVID-19 lockdown periods (2020–2021) at a Scandinavian university and in the post-lockdown period (spring 2022). Findings Teachers reported experiencing feelings of inadequacy due to uncertainty about whether students were benefitting from their teaching in an online environment. We introduce the concept of technoshame to capture this. In addition, our results reveal two emotional challenges related to technoshame, outcome uncertainty and threats to professional identity. Research limitations/implications As an exploratory study, we do not claim to validate technoshame empirically. Future research may further develop the concept and examine its relevance across professions beyond teaching. Practical implications Institutions should strengthen feedback mechanisms in online environments and create peer-based reflection spaces to help professionals navigate feedback-related uncertainty and sustain professional identity. Originality/value This study contributes to literature on shame by introducing the concept of technoshame from an identity-oriented perspective, highlighting previously underexplored emotional challenges in online work-from-home settings.

articles.title: Programmification – the perspective of system rationality
articles.authors: Erik Aal
articles.abstract: Purpose This article contributes to the understanding of programmification. Programmification is not only an organisational phenomenon, commonly referred to as the increasing use of programmes or portfolios of projects, but also an infrastructural one, where an ambient programmification of the public digital sphere occurs. The so-called decentralised autonomous organisations (DAOs) rely on this infrastructural programmification. Design/methodology/approach The article analyses the programmification of conventional organisations and DAOs with the concept of system rationality. It applies the framework that Niklas Luhmann laid out in his timeless, seminal work Zweckbegriff und Systemrationalität. System rationality is based on purpose programmes, which can be shaped in various ways and operate in an informational medium that is created by several complexity reduction strategies. Drawing on a review of available research results, these relevant factors are applied to map the system rationality impact of programmification for conventional organisations and DAOs. Findings System rationality of programmification shows contrasting patterns for conventional organisations and DAOs. Programmification enhances some system rationality factors but limits others. Projectification is closely connected to programmification of conventional organisations, but also an indispensable enabler of DAOs. Originality/value The lens of system rationality offers a deeper insight than what has been so far rendered by studies oriented to managerial and governance aspects. The direct comparison between programmification in these diverging organisational forms answers questions so far not addressed in the literature. The article explains how DAOs can engage in higher complexity products and services. It also argues that project governance within programme structures should mainly be oriented towards communication rather than process compliance.

articles.title: Negotiating algorithmic bias: discourses of techno-optimism and techno-hesitation in AI-mediated hiring
articles.authors: Elisabeth K. Kelan
articles.abstract: Purpose Although artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated hiring is often viewed as a way to reduce human bias, it is commonly singled out as an example of algorithmic bias, which creates and amplifies inequalities. This article explores how the use of AI in hiring can be justified despite the existence of algorithmic bias. Design/methodology/approach Interviews and discourse analysis were conducted to examine how the use of AI in hiring can be justified despite algorithmic bias. Findings The interviewees expressed both techno-optimism and techno-hesitation when talking about AI in hiring. Techno-optimism emphasises that people make hiring processes biased and suggests that algorithmic bias can be addressed through a range of techniques such as fixing the data, fixing the human, “blinding” the algorithm and various processes of quality control and auditing algorithms. Rather than adopting techno-pessimism, the interviewees expressed techno-hesitation. Techno-hesitation refers to the acknowledgement of ethical concerns, followed by their reframing as managerial risks. Techno-optimism and techno-hesitation work together to justify the use of AI in hiring despite the risk of algorithmic bias. Originality/value Through theorising techno-hesitation, this article advances the literature by showing how ethical concerns can function as a resource for sustaining rather than disrupting AI adoption. The study contributes a novel analytical lens for understanding how legitimacy is discursively produced through the management, rather than the resolution, of ethical tensions surrounding AI-mediated hiring.

articles.title: Placing the 5G bets in the early stage: the influence of 5G strategy implementation on credit rating
articles.authors: Xin Bao, Lu Lu, Baiqing Sun, Raymond Lau
articles.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the effect of fifth generation mobile communication technology (5G) strategy implementation on credit ratings and to test the moderating effects of firm attributes on the focal association in the early stage of 5G business application. Design/methodology/approach The research utilized a sample of 573 unique S&P 1500 firms in the early implementation stage of 5G from 2015 to 2020. We then tested the hypotheses with the ordinal logit model. Findings The findings reveal that early-stage 5G strategy implementation negatively impacts credit ratings by increasing default risk and lowering firm value. However, this negative relationship is weakened for firms with higher cash ratios, greater slack, lower capital intensity, and for firms in high-growth industries or with 5G patents. Additionally, firms with 5G strategy implementation face higher bond yields compared to their counterparts. Practical implications This study provides an in-depth understanding of the impact of early-stage 5G strategy implementation on credit ratings for firm managers and capital market participants. Findings help managers navigate early-stage 5G credit constraints, while creditors price these risky strategies based on firm financial attributes. Originality/value This is likely to be the first study that explores the challenges of 5G strategy implementation for credit constraints. The findings of this study reveal that implementing 5G strategies in the early stage tends to signal higher risk-taking incentives. In particular, it highlights resource dependence factors that mitigate the negative impact of 5G strategy implementation on credit ratings.

articles.title: Who to activate next? Predicting influential and susceptible users in social media marketing with CFT-SIS
articles.authors: Syrios Siyao Li, Sufang Wang, Yufei Wu, Yuanyuan Jamie Li, Matthew Kwok On Lee
articles.abstract: Purpose The proliferation of online social networks (OSNs) has brought opportunities and challenges in managing marketing information flows. This study aims to develop an organization-level personalized monitoring model for marketing campaigns, which not only tracks the dynamics of information dissemination but also identifies influential, susceptible and cost-efficient participants to activate in the next round of campaigns. Design/methodology/approach This study develops a novel CFT-SIS framework that integrates curated flows theory (CFT) with the epidemiological susceptible-infected-susceptible (SIS) framework and differentiates information dissemination through broadcasting and narrowcasting channels. It combines users’ susceptibility with their historical influence in brand-specific campaigns to construct the influence-susceptibility index (ISI), precisely measuring both activation difficulty and resulting impact. Findings The CFT-SIS framework enables real-time monitoring of information diffusion by capturing both horizontal spread within individual campaigns and longitudinal interconnections across multiple campaigns. Compared to conventional SIS formulations, it demonstrates higher accuracy and stability in predicting user states. The proposed ISI effectively identifies dual-role users who are both highly influential and easily activated, enabling deeper propagation at lower cost and highlighting participants who drive sustained campaign success. Originality/value This study advances theoretical understanding of sustained social media marketing by identifying a novel and structurally emergent mechanism through which curation hierarchy reshapes user susceptibility and influence across network positions over time. In practice, the model enables the identification of high-impact, easily activated users, supporting more efficient campaign design and resource allocation in social media marketing.

articles.title: Partner Sense of Purpose Predicts Personal and Relational Well-Being in Older Adult Couples
articles.authors: Jason A. Mitala, Brett K. Jakubiak, Yuxi Xie, Brooke C. Feeney
articles.abstract: One’s own sense of purpose is an important predictor of well-being in older adulthood. This research examines whether having a purposeful romantic partner predicts additional enhancements in one’s personal and relational well-being, beyond those explained by one’s own sense of purpose. Both members of older adult romantic couples reported their dispositional sense of purpose and their global well-being, then subsequently reported their daily well-being for seven days. We assessed whether own and partner dispositional sense of purpose predicted well-being (measured globally and measured momentarily in subsequent diary assessments). Beyond effects of one’s own sense of purpose on well-being, partner sense of purpose independently contributed to one’s greater life satisfaction, self-efficacy, relationship satisfaction, and commitment, as well as lower depression, stress, and loneliness (using both global and daily measures). Partner sense of purpose also independently predicted one’s experiences of lower global conflict and daily anxiety. Additional analyses indicated that it is the total purpose in the relationship (and not couples’ similarity in purpose) that predicts these positive outcomes. These findings imply that sense of purpose is a shared resource among older adult couples.

articles.title: Too Late to Trust? Chronemic Expectancy Violations, Appraisal, and Romantic Relationship Trust
articles.authors: Fan Wang
articles.abstract: Depending on the timing of a sensitive admission, a dating partner may view it as candor or withholding. Three hundred thirty-three American adults reported on a dating relationship in which one partner disclosed a clinician-diagnosed mental illness during the first year. Using expectancy violations theory (EVT) and the disclosure processes model (DPM), this study examined associations among disclosure timing, timing appraisal, diagnosis stigma, and latent general trust. A bifactor confirmatory factor analysis of the 17-item trust scale revealed a robust general trust factor. After controlling for baseline trust, relationship tenure, and couple composition, negative-late disclosures were associated with lower latent general trust than on-time disclosures (β = −.27, p < .001). In a mediation model that defined lateness by timing direction alone, perceived timing appropriateness mediated the association between later-than-ideal disclosure and latent general trust, accounting for 28.5% of the total effect. On-time disclosures did not differ from negative-early disclosures or recipient-approved deviations from the ideal. Diagnosis stigma reduced trust independently, although evidence that stigma moderated timing effects was limited. Response surface analysis showed an asymmetric mismatch pattern: trust was lower when disclosure occurred later than the recipient’s ideal than when it occurred earlier, and the fitted surface was mostly linear.

articles.title: Unpacking Loneliness in Europe: Psychosocial and Sociodemographic Correlates Across Regions
articles.authors: Asrin Yenihayat, Mauro Bertolotti, Andrea Bonanomi, Patrizia Catellani
articles.abstract: Perceived loneliness is associated with negative physical and mental health outcomes. Using data from the EU Loneliness Survey, we conducted a path analysis to examine direct and indirect associations between key structural and psychological antecedents of loneliness, and whether these associations differ across European regions. We explored the relationships among sociodemographic factors, health perception, multiple dimensions of social connection, and loneliness. We also tested whether these associations were moderated by macro-level contextual differences, comparing four European regions (Northern, Western, Southern, and Eastern Europe). Results indicated that face-to-face connection, digital connection, and perceived social support were protective against loneliness, whereas social media use was associated with higher loneliness. The effects of sociodemographic characteristics on loneliness were mediated primarily by perceived social support and, to a lesser extent, by health perception, with smaller but significant indirect pathways through face-to-face and digital connections. The effect of digital connection varied by region: it significantly reduced loneliness in Western, Southern, and Eastern Europe, but not in Northern Europe. Social media use was associated with higher loneliness in all regions, with the highest levels in Northern Europe. Overall, these findings suggest that while some protective resources are universal, the benefits of social connection and the risks of social media use vary depending on regional contexts.

articles.title: “It’s Just Still Them”: A Qualitative Study Exploring the Experiences of the Intimate Relational Others of Transgender People
articles.authors: Simaza Sadek
articles.abstract: Research focusing on the intimate relational others (IROs) of transgender people is limited. This study aims to examine the experiences of IROs, especially as they relate to decision-making, relational dynamics, and identity shifts in relationships where a partner comes out as transgender. This study used semi-structured qualitative interviews to examine the experiences of 12 IROs. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to analyze data. IROs were largely unsurprised by their partner’s coming out and reported following the lead of their trans partners about decision-making surrounding coming out to others. IROs acted as a consultant in transition-related decision-making within the relationship and felt protective of their trans partners, especially when they perceived an increasingly hostile environment. IROs reported shifts in their sexual identities that were either related to their partner’s change in identity or facilitated by it. Overall, IROs reported stability in their relationships and highlighted that their relational dynamics and perceptions of their partners remained mostly unchanged. Support for linked lives within the life course perspective and the Gender as Relational model was found. Strengths in the IRO, the trans partner, and the relationship may account for successful navigation of the coming out process.

articles.title: “Thanks for the Clarification”: Denial of Responsibility Is Associated With Better Relationship Quality in Married Couples and Enhanced by Relationship Mindfulness
articles.authors: Daniel K. Smedley, Yunzhi Zheng, Jonathan G. Kimmes
articles.abstract: Although denying responsibility for relationship issues has been theorized as a maladaptive communication behavior, this construct lacks quantitative examination, and alternate theory suggests that denial of responsibility (DOR) may function as a form of direct cooperative communication that adaptively informs a partner’s evaluations of relationship quality, especially when done mindfully. Using a series of actor-partner moderation models (APIMoMs) with a sample of 115 married couples, we examined whether DOR was associated with partner perceptions of relationship quality (partner effects) and whether relationship mindfulness enhances the potential positive effects of DOR. Results showed that DOR was positively associated with better relationship quality, and this association was enhanced when paired with higher relationship mindfulness. These results suggest that DOR can be functional and cooperative, and that relationship mindfulness positively strengthens direct communication. Further replication of these findings may inform clinicians about when to nurture appropriate DOR (i.e., cooperative DOR) or reduce inappropriate DOR (i.e., defensive DOR), and the role of mindfulness in enhancing the potential benefits of DOR.

articles.title: Cynicism Explains the Link Between Subjective Social Class and Perceived Social Support Availability
articles.authors: Gregory T. H. Tan, Jacinth J. X. Tan
articles.abstract: Lower social class individuals tend to report less available support than higher social class individuals. The present research investigated whether lower subjective social class (SSC) individuals may perceive less available support because they are more cynical—or believe that people generally act in their personal interest. Study 1 examined the European Social Survey (Wave 6, N = 54,673) data that assessed individual reports of SSC, cynicism, and perceived social support availability across 29 countries. Path analyses revealed that lower SSC was associated with higher levels of cynicism, which in turn was associated with lower perceived available support. Study 2 sought to replicate the cynicism pathway in the lab and additionally examine if experimentally induced feelings of respect (versus disrespect) may reduce cynicism and increase perceived support availability among lower relative to higher SSC undergraduates ( N = 246). The overall cynicism pathway was replicated, although it was not mitigated by induced feelings of respect. In both studies, the alternative model where perceived support availability explains greater cynicism among lower SSC participants received less support. Our findings preliminarily highlight cynicism as a potential psychological barrier to seeking available social support among lower SSC individuals and the need to explore ways to mitigate cynical worldviews.

articles.title: The Meanings of News: How U.S. Adults Think About the Word “News”
articles.authors: Stephanie Edgerly, Ayse D. Lokmanoglu, Christopher M. Dobmeier, Nathan Walter
articles.abstract: This study explores the immediate, top-of-mind meanings audiences hold about “news.” Inspired by recent audience-centric approaches in defining news, we adopt a schema framework to investigate mental representations of the news concept. Using a national probability survey of U.S. adults, we employ a thought-listing exercise combined with a network analysis. Our findings paint a complex picture of news and its meaning today. We identify six distinct news schemas (i.e., clusters of co-occurring words) that correspond to different audience demographics, political ideology, and news consumption. The findings underscore that news is a dynamic concept with implications for journalism scholarship and practice.

articles.title: Constructing the Journalistic Self: Habitus, Subjectivation, and the Politics of Inequality
articles.authors: Vashan Brown
articles.abstract: How do journalists make sense of themselves and their work in postcolonial societies marked by enduring race and class inequalities? This article examines how journalists discursively represent newsroom dynamics, paying particular attention to how their subjectivities are formed. Drawing on 27 semi-structured in-depth interviews with current and former journalists in Jamaica, this study aims to understand how subjectivation and habitus, shape the ways in which journalists reproduce or contest inequalities. It also examines the professional subjectivities and ideologies that are revealed in the discourse of Jamaican journalists and how they relate to race and class inequalities. Existing work on journalism and inequality has largely focused on questions of voice, whose perspectives are included or excluded, and on how media institutions perpetuate structural inequalities. The findings reveal that journalists’ own subjectivities, social backgrounds, and internalised dispositions shape the way they see themselves and the work that they do. The study identifies a typology of journalistic subjectivities that emerge within postcolonial contexts: the class-conscious journalist, the racially conscious journalist, and the racially neutral journalist.

articles.title: Learning the Limits of Belonging: Classroom-Newsroom Gender Paradox in Nigerian Journalism
articles.authors: Success N. Osayi, Chioma Charity Agboh, Samson Ighiegba Omosotomhe
articles.abstract: We examine women’s dominance in Nigerian journalism classrooms despite their lack of commensurate representation in newsrooms. Drawing on 27 in-depth interviews with female students, we find that journalism is often pursued as a fallback option, limiting initial motivation. Within training institutions, perceptions of poor teaching, lack of practical training, and toxic learning environments appear to contribute to disengagement from the practice. Patriarchal norms, including assumptions about men’s provider role and privileging men’s authority, shape their perception of these discouraging lessons. The findings compound existing pipeline explanations for this disparity, with implications for scholarship on gender equity, journalism pedagogy, and practice.

articles.title: Navigating Precarity: Gendered Labor Inequalities and Economic Vulnerability Among Women Journalists in Ghana
articles.authors: Audrey D. Anchirinah, Danford Zirugo
articles.abstract: Women journalists in Ghana navigate a precarious professional environment marked by job insecurity, prolonged unpaid labor, and systemic gender discrimination within a patriarchal society. This study, based on in-depth qualitative interviews with 27 journalists, explores how precarious employment conditions shape their careers and personal lives. Ghanaian women face increased workplace exploitation, harassment, and career stagnation under weak labor protections. This study contributes to broader discussions on journalism precarity in the Global South, highlighting the need for locally grounded perspectives that reflect the unique sociopolitical and economic realities shaping women’s experiences in media.

articles.title: A Viral War: Threat Perceptions in Light of Social Media News Consumption on the Russo-Ukrainian War
articles.authors: Tamás Tóth, Phelia Weiss, Kevin Koban, Ines Katrin Spielvogel, Jörg Matthes
articles.abstract: This article explores how social media news on the Russo-Ukrainian War shapes people’s perceptions of security through the lens of cultivation theory. Drawing on focus groups ( N = 31), Study 1 shows that Austrian citizens experienced war coverage as immediate but overwhelming, with graphic visuals often triggering anxiety. Study 2, a quota-representative survey ( N = 1,000), finds that frequent exposure to such content heightens Austrians’ perceptions of becoming a victim of this war and makes news appear more emotionally unsettling. Together, we demonstrate that cultivation processes persist in today’s fragmented media environment, with important psychological and societal consequences.

articles.title: Building National Research Infrastructure for Digital Platform Observability at Scale
articles.authors: Bogdan Mamaev, Daniel Angus, Amanda Lawrence, Richard Sinnott
articles.abstract: Digital platforms have fundamentally transformed public communication, yet the capacity to study them is increasingly threatened by restricted data access, opaque algorithmic architectures, and complex legal barriers. Addressing these challenges requires a paradigm shift from isolated, project-based solutions toward shared, national-scale research infrastructures. We present the Australian Internet Observatory (AIO) as a case study of a multi-year initiative designed to facilitate digital media platform observability at scale. The AIO integrates access to computational resources, data governance frameworks, and diverse data sourcing methods, ranging from platform-centric API-harvesting to user-focused data donations. The AIO addresses methodological challenges, ethics, the technical skills gap, and the complexities of regulatory compliance. We argue that shared infrastructures function as vital institutional interventions to ensure independent, reproducible, and ethical digital media research in a continuously evolving media environment

articles.title: Resilience as a Structural Condition: Mental Health and Safety Challenges in Watchdog Science Journalism
articles.authors: Oana Ometa
articles.abstract: This article examines resilience and mental health as structural conditions shaping journalists’ ability to perform a watchdog role in science-related domains. Based on 12 semi-structured interviews with Romanian investigative journalists, the study shows that watchdog science journalism operates in a fragile environment marked by institutional obstruction, financial precarity, harassment, and emotional strain. These pressures are particularly visible in investigations involving public health, environmental issues, and academic integrity, where journalists must deal with restricted access to information, expert authority, and public hostility. Participants describe burnout, anxiety, moral distress, and difficulties in sustaining long-term investigations without institutional support. Although they rely on coping strategies such as therapy, peer support, digital security practices, and professional networks, these mechanisms offer only partial protection. The article argues that resilience should not be understood only as an individual capacity, but as a structural requirement for sustaining watchdog science journalism. Understanding the conditions that undermine journalists’ mental health, safety, and autonomy is essential for assessing the democratic value of their watchdog function.

articles.title: A Research Agenda for Studying LLM-Powered Persuasion Technology to Mitigate Misinformation
articles.authors: Claire Wardle, Pete Brown, David Scales
articles.abstract: Emerging research on the use of large language models (LLMs) to counter false beliefs, including conspiracy theories, vaccine hesitancy, and climate denial, has relied predominantly on experimental methods rooted in social psychology, operationalizing persuasion as short-term attitudinal change measured through randomized controlled trials. We argue that this approach, while offering valuable causal inference, is insufficient for understanding how LLM-powered persuasion actually works. Drawing on communication theory and a qualitative analysis of publicly available transcripts from the “DebunkBot<em> </em>study” (Costello et al., 2024), we identify four constructs largely absent from existing research: users’ mental models of the LLM communicator, anthropomorphism (including negative forms such as attributions of naivety or gullibility that can drive resistance), folk theories about how AI systems operate, and epistemic literacy regarding machine-generated knowledge claims. We outline a research agenda organized around three priorities: methodological pluralism suited to the dynamic and personalized nature of LLM interactions, transparency and reproducibility standards for prompt design and transcript analysis, and ethical frameworks for assessing potential harms, including belief reinforcement among resistant participants and privacy risks in large-scale transcript data.

articles.title: Transparency is a Double-Edged Sword: Stakeholders’ Perception of GenAI Usage Disclosure in Kenyan Newsrooms
articles.authors: Bingbing Zhang, Kevin C. Mudavadi, Chenghan Zhou
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been increasingly adopted globally in journalism, raising critical ethical considerations, especially regarding the transparency of its usage in news production. Existing research shows that disclosing AI authorship or involvement in news writing affects news audiences’ perceived trustworthiness and credibility, with most studies conducted in the Global North. However, current research has primarily focused on news audiences, overlooking other key stakeholders, such as journalists and policymakers, who also shape ethical norms and practices surrounding AI transparency in journalism. Furthermore, research on GenAI in journalism remains heavily focused on the Global North, leaving significant gaps in understanding how stakeholders in the Global South perceive and evaluate GenAI disclosure in journalistic content. In response, we conducted 94 in-depth interviews with six groups in Kenya—news audiences, journalists, policymakers, influencers, journalism educators, and information technology experts—to examine how stakeholders in Kenya perceive GenAI disclosure in journalistic content and the extent to which they trust news stories generated by AI or assisted by AI. Our analysis shows a “double-edged sword effect”: While most stakeholders advocated for transparency about GenAI use in journalism, many journalists expressed concern that such disclosure could undermine the perceived authenticity and credibility of news content. Such distrust stemmed from ethical concerns that overreliance on GenAI could lead to “less human” journalism and the spread of unverified or biased GenAI content. Stakeholders also expressed conditional trust that varies depending on the type of story, the level of GenAI use, and the nature of the content.

articles.title: Hybrid Moderation in Practice: How Users, AI, and Professionals Judge Uncivil Comments
articles.authors: Aviv Barnoy
articles.abstract: Online platforms increasingly rely on hybrid moderation systems that combine automated triage with professional human review, yet little research compares how these actors judge the same real content in production-linked settings. This article examines uncivil online comments as a platform-governance problem by comparing three decision-makers: registered users, a platform AI system, and professional moderators. Using a secondary dataset from a US-based publisher comment environment, we analyze real comments spanning five moderation categories: Violence, Doxxing, Hate Speech, Sexual Explicitness, and Personal Attacks. The dataset combines production-stage AI workflow dispositions, professional moderators’ final adjudications, and ex-post survey judgments from 863 registered users, yielding 8,588 user-comment decisions. Results show that users chose to allow publication of roughly two-thirds of the uncivil comments and that their decisions aligned more closely with the AI system’s publish-and-moderate versus hold-and-moderate orientation than with professional moderators’ publish-versus-block decisions. Divergence was concentrated in specific categories and items, especially Hate Speech. Users’ justifications suggest that permissive decisions often relied on threshold reasoning, rejection of toxicity, or free-speech concerns, whereas restrictive decisions more often relied on direct violation labels. Demographic and engagement-based predictors explained little variance in alignment. The findings suggest that users, AI systems, and professional moderators should not be treated as interchangeable moderation tools: they operationalize different thresholds and may be suited to different governance functions.

articles.title: Fact-Checking With Machines: Journalism Students’ Perceptions of AI and the Ethics of Counterspeech
articles.authors: Yearry Panji Setianto
articles.abstract: This article examines how journalism students in Indonesia negotiate the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into fact-checking and counterspeech practices within journalism education. Drawing on practice theory, the study conceptualizes AI as part of the material dimension of journalistic practice and explores how its use reconfigures the relationships between materials, competence, and meanings. The study draws on elicitation interviews in which students explored conventional and AI-assisted fact-checking and reflected on how each shaped their verification practices. The findings show that students adopt a hybrid approach, using AI to enhance efficiency without replacing established verification routines grounded in mainstream media and official sources. While AI tools highlight time-saving capabilities and assist in generating counterspeech, students continue to rely on traditional methods in situations requiring greater human judgement. This suggests that AI is integrated as a complementary resource rather than a substitute for journalistic judgment. However, AI-assisted fact-checking practices raise concerns about the erosion of critical evaluation skills. More importantly, the findings reveal tensions in the meanings underpinning journalistic practice. Students frame fact-checking and counterspeech as ethical and interpretive activities, emphasizing transparency, responsibility, and authenticity. Overall, the study argues that AI integration reshapes not only the workflows but also the normative foundations of fact-checking and public engagement, highlighting the need for human-centered and ethically grounded journalism education.

articles.title: Presumed media influence and support for social media bans: The roles of social and elite-based validation
articles.authors: Sarah Geber, Anne Schulz, Mike S. Schäfer, Thomas N. Friemel
articles.abstract: The study examines how presumed influences of social media on young people, as well as perceptions of how widely such beliefs are shared, shape support for social media bans. Extending the Influence of Presumed Influence (IPI) model, we introduce second-order presumed influences, defined as perceptions about how widely others presume media influences, and propose a mechanism of social validation. We additionally examine elite-based validation, referring to perceived beliefs of influential actors (i.e. scientists, politicians, and the media), as well as perceived social norms. Using survey data ( N = 1270) collected in the context of debates about a social media ban for minors under 16 in Switzerland, we find that stronger presumed influences predict support for a ban. While we find no support for social validation, the results point to the relevance of elite-related perceptions, particularly presumed scientific consensus. Perceived social norms of ban support emerge as an additional predictor of regulatory preferences.

articles.title: The role of AI competencies: How do AI knowledge, skills, and attitudes shape users’ understanding and evaluation of explainable news recommendations?
articles.authors: Chenyue Wang, Anne C. Kroon, Judith Möller, Claes H. de Vreese, Sophie C. Boerman
articles.abstract: This study investigates how explanations in AI-driven news recommender systems (RS) influence user understanding, trust, and attitudes toward the RS, and whether these effects depend on individual differences in AI competence. An online experiment ( N = 754) was conducted in the Netherlands with a no-explanation condition as baseline. Results show that joint explanations significantly improved users’ objective understanding of the RS but had no consistent direct effects on perceived understanding, trust, or attitudes toward the RS. Exploratory structural equation modeling revealed an indirect pathway in which explanations enhanced objective understanding, which increased perceived understanding, subsequently fostering greater trust and more positive attitudes. Moderation analyses showed limited evidence for AI competence conditioning explanation effects, with small benefits concentrated among users with higher AI knowledge. Together, these findings suggest that explanations in news RS are not universally effective: their effects appear to operate primarily through cognitive mechanisms, while competence-related differences remain limited and selective.

articles.title: Do WhatsApp news channels help users navigate the information environment? A field experiment on information-related attitudes
articles.authors: Camila Mont’Alverne, Patrícia Rossini, Antonis Kalogeropoulos
articles.abstract: Messaging applications have become central sources of news, especially in the Global South, raising concerns about the quality of information circulating in these spaces. This study examines how receiving news through WhatsApp channels shapes key information-related attitudes in Brazil, including misinformation belief, news fatigue, and media trust. In a pre‑registered experiment conducted in November/December 2024, 601 participants from multiple Brazilian states were asked to subscribe to either a regional news channel or a fact‑checking channel operated by Globo, the largest media group in Latin America. The results show that accessing news via WhatsApp does not alter more stable attitudes, such as belief in misinformation or trust. However, it does reduce news fatigue and increases engagement with news on WhatsApp. As news consumption shifts toward private messaging platforms, these findings suggest their value lies less in reshaping political attitudes and more in maintaining routine connections between audiences and journalism.

articles.title: “You can’t challenge the narrative”: Conservative-leaning New Zealanders on power, truth and politics in science
articles.authors: Alex Beattie, Natalia Albert, Shona Riddell
articles.abstract: Institutions shape ideas and bridge gaps between competing views, but their role in managing tensions within scientific communities is under-researched. This paper uses social cohesion and new institutionalism frameworks to explore conservative New Zealanders’ perspectives that compete with dominant institutional scientific narratives. We conducted semi-structured interviews with conservative-leaning New Zealanders, enquiring about their perspectives on the politics and practice of science in Aotearoa New Zealand. We found a strong belief in the importance of science and a high regard for scientists, provided they maintain objectivity and challenge prevailing ideas, alongside concerns about institutional bias and outspoken scientists being cancelled by institutions. We discuss how these themes undermine social cohesion, with perceived institutional bias eroding vertical cohesion—trust between groups and institutions—and leading to the emergence of parallel alternative institutions that break horizontal cohesion—trust between groups in society.

articles.title: When scientists ‘Tok: Memetic communication and scientific information engagement in short video-based social media
articles.authors: Jon Benedik Bunquin, Alex Segrè Cohen
articles.abstract: TikTok has rapidly emerged as an influential platform for science communication, particularly among younger audiences. Its affordances encourage memetic communication—characterized by imitation, humor, and participatory storytelling—offering scientists novel ways to engage publics. Our study explores scientists’ use of memetic elements on TikTok and their associations with audience engagement. Drawing on social media logic and platform vernacular theories, we conducted a quantitative content analysis of 1025 science-related videos from 113 TikTok creators. Findings revealed widespread use of emotional and conversational language, but fewer videos incorporated reappropriated media or collectivist storytelling. Multilevel models showed that imitation and humor positively predicted likes, shares, comments, and views, whereas reappropriation negatively predicted engagement metrics. These results underscore the importance of aligning science communication strategies with platform-specific vernaculars. We discuss implications for public science engagement in digital, algorithmically driven environments, where visibility and audience trust increasingly depend on culturally resonant and participatory content.

articles.title: When academic leaders disconnect from social media in Finland: Situational rationality, silent resistance
articles.authors: Leena Ripatti-Torniainen, Karoliina Talvitie-Lamberg
articles.abstract: This qualitative study, conducted at Finland’s research universities, analyses high-profile academic leaders who have chosen to be disconnected from social media. We conducted individual interviews with 19 leaders and performed a situational analysis to investigate the rationale for abstaining from social media. Academic leaders rationalised disconnection by reasons related to personality, sociability, critical rationality, and health and security. The leaders’ intensive involvement in three social worlds intensified the individual rationale for disconnection and enabled the leaders to work successfully despite disconnection. These social worlds were research and science, sensitive academia, and insider networks in society. In the context of the managerial neoliberal university, its promotional communication culture, and competition for visibility, the leaders’ disconnection from social media has a dissident, resistant characteristic. The study contributes to prior research through its comprehensive approach to academic leaders’ operational environment. Future research should elaborate on the systemic approach to social media in universities.

articles.title: Accuracy and Defense Motives: Exploring Types of Information Insufficiency in the Risk Information Seeking and Processing (RISP) Model
articles.authors: Timothy K. F. Fung, Ho Man Leung, Po Yan Lai, Robert J. Griffin
articles.abstract: This study reconceptualizes information insufficiency as a goal-contingent construct within the Risk Information Seeking and Processing model. In multifaceted risk contexts, individuals confront health threats alongside challenges to deep-seated values and beliefs, producing different judgmental demands within a single risk event. Survey data from 858 Hong Kong adults show two distinct forms of information insufficiency, one oriented toward accurate safety judgments and another toward defending deep-seated values and beliefs. Each form is associated with distinct patterns of information seeking and processing. This study demonstrates how multiple goal-based information insufficiencies operate within the same individual in response to different judgmental demands.

articles.title: Forming Relationships With Scientists Through Film: A Qualitative Study of Viewers’ Trust, Identification, and Value Alignment
articles.authors: Nicole M. Krause, Emily L. Howell, Sarah S. Goodwin
articles.abstract: Drawing on open-ended responses from a national U.S. survey ( N = 630) of viewers of Observer , a documentary film featuring scientists engaged in practices of observation, we examine how audiences explained trust, identification, and perceived value alignment with the film’s characters, most of whom were explicitly identified as scientists. Participants most often cited relational and affective qualities—curiosity, authenticity, attentiveness, and communication style—rather than formal expertise or social identities. Findings distinguish trust, identification, and value alignment as distinct forms of affinity, and illustrate the relational, affective, and experiential reasoning audiences drew on when articulating connection with scientists in this context.

articles.title: Anthropomorphizing AI: Perceptions, Interpretations, and the Humanization of Generative AI
articles.authors: Mohammad Hossein Jarrahi, Amir Karami, Lisa Park, Ensieh Jarrahi, Christoph Lutz
articles.abstract: The rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly advanced AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, has transformed human–AI interactions by providing unprecedentedly natural interaction environments. These developments have significantly heightened user perceptions of AI as human-like, making anthropomorphism, a tendency to attribute human traits to non-humans, increasingly prevalent. Despite the recognition of the rising anthropomorphism in these interaction modalities, little is known about how people anthropomorphize generative AI, especially in social media discourse. Using Twitter/X as a discursive space, we systematically analyze how users described and engaged with ChatGPT, identifying distinct categories and recurring forms of anthropomorphism. Findings reveal diverse anthropomorphic perceptions, including personification, emotional attributions, cognitive and human-like attributes, social interactions, and human-like personality traits. Building on the observation that social media platforms not only reflect but also actively shape and reinforce anthropomorphic narratives, this study raises important implications for trust, misinformation, user expectations, and human–AI interactions.

articles.title: When Herstory Goes Viral: Popular Resistance in the State-Platform Nexus in China
articles.authors: Qingyue Sun, Runze Ding
articles.abstract: This article examines the rise of herstory content on Douyin to explore how feminist resistance takes shape within China’s platform environment. Drawing on digital ethnography, we develop the concept of popular resistance, a form of platform-mediated resistance whose popularity serves both as a condition of political traction and as a mechanism of containment. To clarify this duality, we identify two dimensions: (a) popularity on the platform, driven by trends, aestheticization, and commodification; and (b) popularity within orthodoxy, shaped by state-sanctioned values that render certain forms of feminist expression politically permissible. Popular resistance retains a critical, if slippery, edge. It gives voice to gendered injustices while remaining entangled with the algorithmic, commercial, and political infrastructures that simultaneously enable and discipline it. We conclude by proposing popular resistance as a transferable analytic for understanding how political expression in the digital age gains visibility, negotiates power, and persists within the very systems that constrain it.
